rationale: Selected one-symbol EOD slice: four source items trace to defined L1/L2/L3 contracts. Typed numeric/Table implementation is experimental with partial synthetic evidence; full acceptance and live service behavior remain unverified. See docs/requirements/stock-eod-evidence.md for deviations and gates.
The exact 14-member wheel is inventoried and licensed source provenance is retained; this does not claim that the Python distribution installs correctly or is published by this Rust project.

Raw descriptor types and 82 service bindings are preserved by Rust code generation. This status covers wire shape only; query defaults, server availability, entitlements, and complete typed API behavior remain unverified.

The Python Client follows the vendor's credential order and constructor options, and can share an existing session without logging in again. Rust keeps auth, storage and async client construction separate on purpose; there is no single Rust constructor that mirrors Python's.

The common two-line email/password input is supported. Python returns None for absent/empty files and conflates those at the caller; Rust intentionally returns explicit errors. This is input compatibility, not identical Python exception behavior.

API-key/email-password JSON, environment envelope, and session parsing are implemented with synthetic tests. Rust validates required strings, preserves optional subscription JSON, and deliberately differs from Python malformed-response/logging behavior. Live auth is unverified.

Rust sessions can be passed explicitly without repeated login. Native persistence is an intentional project addition, not Python parity. Vendor expiry, invalidation, or cross-environment portability are not established.
Implicit .env loading is deliberately excluded by the accepted auth contract. CLI environment discovery remains explicit; the library does not inspect the process environment.
Do not reproduce Python's INFO dump of the successful identity response or raw rejection text. Rust redacts credential/session secrets and does not echo server bodies.

All 81 vendor wrappers exist as generated Rust requests (endpoints::*, with the vendor's defaults and explicit presence) and as same-name Python methods with the vendor 1.0.17 signatures (tested). Live: 50 of the 51 option wrappers are value-checked on options PRO (columnar against legacy decoder, plus the Python package); the option quote flat file is gated on size. The 30 stock, index, calendar and interest-rate wrappers have only the one-time FREE entitlement map (6 entitled, 11 tier-denied, 13 not probed) and no value checks; see docs/endpoints/coverage.md. Requests carry typed wire fields; there is no per-endpoint validation of argument values beyond their types.

Generated requests format dates, times and expirations the way the wrappers do (typed Expiration, TimeOfDay and Symbols, including the * wildcard). The Python package accepts datetime.date or YYYY-MM-DD, datetime.time or vendor text, and refuses a datetime where a date is expected rather than dropping its time. Per-method differences follow the generated wrapper rules; vendor behaviour for malformed text is not reproduced.

Optional request fields are Option<T> with the vendor's defaults, and the wrappers' truthiness guards are applied as the vendor applies them (tested per shape: snapshots, OHLC intervals, Greeks). In Python, passing a default builds the same wire query as omitting it. This is wire-level compatibility with the wrapper, checked synthetically; server-side defaults are not inferred.

Python sends parameter strings plus client=python in QueryInfo; Rust currently sends client=rust and token/email only. Privacy policy, diagnostics, and version fields need an explicit compatibility decision.

query() and job() run on a tier-aware scheduler (PRO 8 concurrent, FREE 1 and 20 per minute by default, overridable), with deadlines, idle timeouts and cancellation; jobs split by date and, for all-strike fine quotes, by strike, with ordered read-ahead. Only RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED and UNAVAILABLE are retried, and only when a request opens. Measured live up to 8 concurrent on options PRO; behaviour above 8 and over the vendor's limits is not probed.

Rust maps failures to typed QueryError classes: remote status, decode/schema errors, timeouts, cancellation and SessionEnded for UNAUTHENTICATED on every path. Rows received before a failure are delivered, then the error once. Python raises ThetaDataError subclasses (QueryFailed, SessionEnded, OutputFailed). The vendor's exception classes and messages are not reproduced; this is a deliberate, documented difference.

A columnar decoder turns each response into Arrow record batches (exact types, nulls backfilled, schema errors classified) and query() coalesces them into batches; Python and Parquet output build on the same batches. Values are checked equal to the legacy decoder live on 50 option RPCs. A batch stream is not one accumulated dataframe; Result and collect() accumulate explicitly.

Prices are exact decimal128(38, 10) in Arrow, from the wire mantissa and scale, never floats. This deliberately differs from Python's float multiplication and NaN. Values match the legacy decoder on the live option checks.

The Arrow path emits millisecond timestamps with their time zone, as Polars and pandas expect, and rejects mixed zones in one column. The legacy Table adapter still formats RFC3339 strings. Nanosecond precision stays open under ADR-0019 until ThetaData defines nanos and precision.

The Python package returns the client's dataframe_type (Polars by default, pandas or Arrow) for vendor-named methods, and Result.to_polars/to_pandas/to_arrow otherwise, through the Arrow PyCapsule interface without per-row Python objects. Column types are exact (decimal prices, zone-aware timestamps), so they differ from the vendor's float columns. Rust stays Arrow-only, with no Python dependency.

DecodeLimits bound every message and the decoder's buffer, and the streaming path (job to Parquet) was measured live with a Rust heap bounded by configuration plus Parquet footer metadata of about 13 KB per row group. On the query path the bound also includes up to streams × encoded_bytes for messages being assembled, only while they are in flight (item 8, closed 2026-11-10). This does not bound total process memory, and an accumulated Result grows with its rows.

Flat-file responses decode through the same columnar path into Parquet. Live, the option open-interest, EOD and trade-quote files were downloaded in full and decoded with no error or manifest, values compared on the first message. The option quote file (about 38 GB) is gated on the user's go-ahead; the stock and index flat files are not checked. Like Python, the manifest is not used.

Dividend and split RPCs each accept symbol/start_date/end_date and stream ResponseData, but have no Python wrapper or operation in the previously reviewed OpenAPI. Preserve bindings without promising supported service behavior.

Seventeen GetFuture* RPCs (1.0.16) have request/response descriptors and generated stubs but no Python wrapper, OpenAPI operation or public documentation. Preserve raw bindings without promising supported service behavior, symbology, entitlements or result schemas.

Do not port Python-specific generated stub/server/experimental helper implementations into a Rust client. Every symbol is inventoried; their RPC signatures and wire paths are preserved separately in Rust generation. This excludes language scaffolding, not market-data capabilities.

dotenv is imported but not declared; generated gRPC requires >=1.80.0 despite metadata >=1.75.0; ZoneInfo needs timezone data. Record these packaging/runtime assumptions without reproducing Python dependency defects in Rust.
Preserve all eleven embedded Python examples as evidence and review parameter/return assumptions. They are source examples, not executed live acceptance tests or approved Rust API designs.

Expiry, refresh, revocation, IP binding, entitlement interpretation, token reuse limits, and identity quotas have no complete observed contract. Do not derive them from local persistence or Terminal REST documentation.

The Python artifact has no streaming client; finite gRPC query streams are a different thing. Rust adds a separate adapter for the operator-run Terminal's WebSocket (ADR-0018): quotes and the full trade stream, verified on the Terminal's dev feed, and for option quotes on the live market (2026-11-10). The live full trade stream ran with 0 dropped at midday and across the close run-up (Windows), and under WSL2 (with a p99 above the target there); native Linux remains, so this stays unresolved as parity, and it is not a missing wrapper inferred from server_streaming=true.
